source.title: A Closer Look at Multimodal Representation Collapse
source.authors: Abhra Chaudhuri; Anjan Dutta; Bui Tu; Serban Georgescu

record.tranche_reason: Tests cross-modal polysemanticity and its consequences using multimodal fusion experiments and a modality-classifier cross-entropy measure, rather than the original neuron-level visualization method.
record.gate_note: Table 9 directly measures cross-modal polysemanticity using the authors’ modality-classifier cross-entropy. Table 10 reports semantic-loss results that the authors relate to modality collapse as the number of modalities increases. Other rank, VIF, and benchmark results were not recorded unless they directly bear on a listed version. Results cited from prior work are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper explicitly presupposes polysemanticity (more task-relevant features than neurons) and uses it to explain modality collapse in multimodal fusion heads. Its only polysemanticity-related number (Table 9) is a weight-level modality-classifier cross-entropy. This proxy measures uncertainty in assigning fusion-head weights to a modality, not neurons responding to unrelated inputs, and it is not a share of polysemantic neurons. The semantic-loss, rank and AUC results measure modality collapse or the study's own method's performance, not polysemanticity. No version is tested by a measure of the behaviour the versions name. The paper also never varies features relative to neuron count, so V3 is not tested either.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that low-rank gradient updates force fusion-head neurons to polysemantically entangle predictive features of one modality with noisy features of another, causing modality collapse. They argue that KD implicitly frees rank bottlenecks and that EBR does so explicitly, reducing collapse and improving missing-modality performance. Polysemanticity itself is presupposed, not shown to arise from capacity pressure.
record.recipe_differences: Uses theory about rank bottlenecks and multimodal fusion experiments, including a modality-classifier cross-entropy proxy and basis-reallocation interventions; it does not reproduce the original neuron-visualization method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported semantic-loss gap varies with the number of modalities. The cross-modal CE measurement also varies with the training method (vanilla, KD, EBR).

fits_no_version.finding: A modality classifier applied to fusion-head weights shows lower output cross-entropy after KD (2.09) and EBR (0.59) than vanilla training (5.66). The authors read this as reduced cross-modal polysemanticity in bi-modal MIMIC-IV fusion heads.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-modal polysemanticity in multimodal fusion heads, measured as modality-assignment uncertainty of weights, falls under basis-reallocation training (KD, EBR) while task performance improves.

fits_no_version.finding: The semantic-loss gap between the collapsed modality's encoder and its unimodal baseline grows with the number of modalities (27.68 vs 7.97 at 2 modalities; 167.30 vs 9.55 at 5). The authors attribute this to cross-modal polysemantic interference, but polysemanticity is not measured directly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Modality collapse in multimodal fusion worsens with more modalities, attributed (theoretically) to cross-modal polysemantic interference.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of the 42nd ICML, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The paper states that its results presuppose polysemanticity, including more task-relevant features than neurons, and some theoretical results assume equal feature information. The empirical polysemanticity measure is a modality-classifier CE proxy, with no uncertainty reported for Table 9. The study does not directly inspect individual neuron activations or establish that capacity pressure is necessary. The mortality AUC-PRC EBR entry in Table 1 is malformed as printed and was not extracted.
record.rows_left_out: The malformed mortality AUC-PRC EBR value in Table 1 (Section 4.4) was not recorded. Other performance metrics, ranks, representation similarities, VIF values, and noise-rate plots were left out because they do not directly measure neuron polysemanticity or a listed version’s specific behavior.

untested.parts: The paper assumes superposition and never varies the number of features relative to neurons. It does not measure whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
There is no count or share of polysemantic neurons across activation functions, architectures or regularizers. The KD/EBR change is shown only on a weight-level CE proxy.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites polysemanticity and superposition (Elhage 2022, Scherlis 2022, Lecomte 2024) as theoretical tools and states that its results presuppose polysemanticity. Table 9 has no uncertainty and gives no detail on per-neuron assignment. A lenient reader might link r1–r3 to V5 as weak support (training choice lowers a polysemanticity proxy without performance loss). That link rests on an indirect weight-classifier measure in multimodal fusion MLPs, so it is recorded here as fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier neurons or vision-model polysemanticity are tested.
No transformer language models, language-model MLP neurons, or token/context responses are tested.

The study focuses on cross-modal fusion neurons. It does not directly vary the number of features relative to neuron capacity or test whether excess feature capacity is necessary for the measured polysemanticity; the paper states that its results presuppose polysemanticity.
Initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity without capacity pressure are not tested.
The study tests knowledge distillation and Explicit Basis Reallocation, not SoLU, modern convnets, or a systematic comparison of activation functions and architectures.
The study does not use improved neuron explanations to test whether canonical mixtures share one semantic feature or whether truly unrelated mixtures are rare.
The study does not vary activation-range slices or explanation-scoring methods to test measurement dependence.

rows.subject: MIMIC-IV multimodal fusion head (specific model not stated)
rows.operation_detail: A two-layer ReLU modality classifier was applied to fusion-head weights; average output cross-entropy was used as the cross-modal polysemanticity measure.
rows.measure: Average cross-entropy (CE) of modality-classifier outputs; the authors interpret higher CE as greater cross-modal polysemanticity.
rows.note: The paper reports this as the vanilla comparison; no chance level or uncertainty is given.
rows.check: The CE is a modality-classifier uncertainty on fusion-head weights: a proxy for cross-modal 'capacity allocation'. It is not a share of neurons responding to unrelated inputs. It has no baseline, chance level or uncertainty, and it cannot show V3's causal claim.

rows.subject: MIMIC-IV multimodal fusion head (specific model not stated)
rows.operation_detail: The same modality-classifier cross-entropy measure was applied after knowledge distillation.
rows.measure: Average cross-entropy (CE) of modality-classifier outputs; the authors interpret lower CE relative to vanilla as reduced cross-modal polysemanticity.
rows.note: The authors describe the lower relative CE as indicating reduced cross-modal polysemantic interference.
rows.check: Same proxy measure (KD 2.09 vs vanilla 5.66). It bears on a related construct, not on V3 or V5 as named; recorded under fits_no_version. No uncertainty is reported.

rows.subject: MIMIC-IV multimodal fusion head (specific model not stated)
rows.operation_detail: The same modality-classifier cross-entropy measure was applied after Explicit Basis Reallocation.
rows.measure: Average cross-entropy (CE) of modality-classifier outputs; the authors interpret lower CE relative to vanilla as reduced cross-modal polysemanticity.
rows.note: The authors describe the lower relative CE as indicating reduced cross-modal polysemantic interference.
rows.check: Same proxy measure (EBR 0.59 vs vanilla 5.66). EBR is the authors' own method; recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: GMC on MIMIC-IV
rows.operation_detail: A contrastive objective was used; the study reports the lowest achieved training semantic loss for the multimodal prefix.
rows.note: The authors describe the multimodal-prefix versus unimodal-baseline gap as consistent with the modality undergoing collapse contributing less to the downstream representation.
rows.check: Semantic loss of the collapsed modality's encoder measures modality collapse, not neuron polysemanticity or its cause. Linking it to V3 relies on the authors' interpretation only.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Bi-modal MIMIC-IV fusion heads, vanilla versus KD and EBR
reader_labels.reason: The authors’ operational measure of cross-modal polysemanticity decreases from 5.66 for vanilla to 2.09 with KD and 0.59 with EBR (r1–r3); the GMC semantic-loss results also show a widening multimodal-prefix gap as modalities increase (r4, r6, r8, r10).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: MIMIC-IV bi-modal cross-entropy measurement and MIMIC-IV missingness benchmark
reader_labels.reason: KD and EBR have lower modality-classifier CE than vanilla (r1–r3), and EBR improves the reported readmission AUC-ROC and AUC-PRC results relative to MUSE (r13–r14). The mortality AUC-ROC result also improves (r12).
